claim: The spatial tuning of neuronal populations in the early visual cortical regions is related to the spatial frequency (SF) selectivity of neurons.
source: The spatial tuning of neuronal populations in the early visual cortical regions is related to the spatial frequency (SF) selectivity of neurons.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis and conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental results showing pRF size changes following SF adaptation.

claim: Adaptation to low SF resulted in smaller pRFs.
source: Results showed that adaptation to a low/high SF resulted in smaller/larger pRFs, respectively, as hypothesised.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI experiment, supported by data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Adaptation to high SF resulted in larger pRFs.
source: Results showed that adaptation to a low/high SF resulted in smaller/larger pRFs, respectively, as hypothesised.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI experiment, supported by data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Receptive fields are organized such that adjacent neurons are stimulated by adjacent areas in the visual field.
source: The receptive fields are organized in such a way that adjacent neurons are stimulated by adjacent areas in the visual field (Wandell et al., 2005; Wandell and Winawer, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Receptive field characteristics of the human visual cortex can be studied with a model-based pRF mapping method using fMRI.
source: A consequence of such retinotopic organisation is that receptive field characteristics of the human visual cortex can be studied with a model-based pRF mapping method (Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008) using fMRI.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the foundational pRF mapping methodology.

claim: Receptive field sizes of neuronal populations depend on the eccentricity of the receptive field location.
source: Both pRF mapping (Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008; Amano et al., 2009; Dumoulin and Harvey, 2012) and electrophysiology (Van Essen et al., 1984; Klink et al., 2021) studies have established that the receptive field sizes of neuronal populations depend on (a) the eccentricity of the receptive field location and (b) the visual area they are drawn from, within the visual hierarchy.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to both pRF mapping and electrophysiology studies.

claim: Receptive field sizes of neuronal populations depend on the visual area they are drawn from within the visual hierarchy.
source: Both pRF mapping (Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008; Amano et al., 2009; Dumoulin and Harvey, 2012) and electrophysiology (Van Essen et al., 1984; Klink et al., 2021) studies have established that the receptive field sizes of neuronal populations depend on (a) the eccentricity of the receptive field location and (b) the visual area they are drawn from, within the visual hierarchy.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to both pRF mapping and electrophysiology studies.

claim: Neurons corresponding to the central visual field exhibit smaller receptive fields (finer spatial tuning).
source: Neurons corresponding to the central visual field exhibit smaller receptive fields (finer spatial tuning), whereas those responding to the more peripheral visual field have larger receptive fields (coarser spatial tuning).
evidence: This is established knowledge in visual neuroscience, implied by the context and citations in the surrounding text.

claim: Neurons responding to the more peripheral visual field have larger receptive fields (coarser spatial tuning).
source: Neurons corresponding to the central visual field exhibit smaller receptive fields (finer spatial tuning), whereas those responding to the more peripheral visual field have larger receptive fields (coarser spatial tuning).
evidence: This is established knowledge in visual neuroscience, implied by the context and citations in the surrounding text.

claim: A progressive increase in eccentricity is associated with a proportional decline in resolution visual acuity.
source: A progressive increase in eccentricity is associated with a proportional decline in resolution visual acuity (Anstis, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Perceived size biases in eccentric areas of the visual field are linked to the spatial tuning pattern across eccentricity.
source: Additionally, perceived size biases in eccentric areas of the visual field are linked to the spatial tuning pattern across eccentricity (Moutsiana et al., 2016; Urale and Schwarzkopf, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neurons in early visual areas are selectively sensitive to a limited range of spatial frequencies within their receptive fields.
source: Neurons in early visual areas are selectively sensitive to a limited range of spatial frequencies (SFs) within their receptive fields.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the citations that follow in the text.

claim: SF tuning in the visual cortex has been reported in cats.
source: SF tuning in the visual cortex has been reported in cats (Everson et al., 1998; Hübener et al., 1997), macaque monkeys (Xu et al., 2007; De Valois et al., 1982), and humans using fMRI (Aghajari et al., 2020; Henriksson et al., 2008; Broderick et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: SF tuning in the visual cortex has been reported in macaque monkeys.
source: SF tuning in the visual cortex has been reported in cats (Everson et al., 1998; Hübener et al., 1997), macaque monkeys (Xu et al., 2007; De Valois et al., 1982), and humans using fMRI (Aghajari et al., 2020; Henriksson et al., 2008; Broderick et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: SF tuning in the visual cortex has been reported in humans using fMRI.
source: SF tuning in the visual cortex has been reported in cats (Everson et al., 1998; Hübener et al., 1997), macaque monkeys (Xu et al., 2007; De Valois et al., 1982), and humans using fMRI (Aghajari et al., 2020; Henriksson et al., 2008; Broderick et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Prolonged exposure to a grating of a particular SF reduces perceptual sensitivity to the adapted SF, which manifests as an increase in the detection threshold for a grating at the adapted SF.
source: Prolonged exposure to a grating of a particular SF (1) reduces perceptual sensitivity to the adapted SF, which manifests as an increase in the detection threshold for a grating at the adapted SF; and (2) alters the apparent SF of subsequently presented gratings such that their apparent SF is 'repelled' from the adapted SF (i.e. lower SF gratings appear even lower, higher SF gratings appear even higher; see Webster, 2015 for a review on visual adaptation).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review on visual adaptation.

claim: Prolonged exposure to a grating of a particular SF alters the apparent SF of subsequently presented gratings such that their apparent SF is 'repelled' from the adapted SF.
source: Prolonged exposure to a grating of a particular SF (1) reduces perceptual sensitivity to the adapted SF, which manifests as an increase in the detection threshold for a grating at the adapted SF; and (2) alters the apparent SF of subsequently presented gratings such that their apparent SF is 'repelled' from the adapted SF (i.e. lower SF gratings appear even lower, higher SF gratings appear even higher; see Webster, 2015 for a review on visual adaptation).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review on visual adaptation.

claim: The SF adaptation effect suggests the existence of SF tuning channel units, each maximally sensitive to a given relatively narrow range of SFs.
source: This adaptation effect suggests the existence of SF tuning channel units, each maximally sensitive to a given relatively narrow range of SFs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the adaptation effects described, supported by citations in the following sentence.

claim: A decline in one channel's sensitivity results in the adjacent channels taking the lead in the overall response, thereby shifting the perceived SF.
source: A decline in one channel's sensitivity results in the adjacent channels taking the lead in the overall response, thereby shifting the perceived SF (Braddick et al., 1978; Mollon, 1974; Frisby and Mayhew, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A similar channel mechanism has been proposed to account for eccentric size aftereffects.
source: A similar channel mechanism has been proposed to account for eccentric size aftereffects (Altan and Boyaci, 2020) and numerosity adaptation (Aulet and Lourenco, 2023), although others have claimed SF channels themselves play a direct role in numerosity judgments (Dakin et al., 2011; Paul et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A similar channel mechanism has been proposed to account for numerosity adaptation.
source: A similar channel mechanism has been proposed to account for eccentric size aftereffects (Altan and Boyaci, 2020) and numerosity adaptation (Aulet and Lourenco, 2023), although others have claimed SF channels themselves play a direct role in numerosity judgments (Dakin et al., 2011; Paul et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Some researchers have claimed SF channels themselves play a direct role in numerosity judgments.
source: A similar channel mechanism has been proposed to account for eccentric size aftereffects (Altan and Boyaci, 2020) and numerosity adaptation (Aulet and Lourenco, 2023), although others have claimed SF channels themselves play a direct role in numerosity judgments (Dakin et al., 2011; Paul et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Studies have suggested that SF-tuned mechanisms play a crucial role in size perception.
source: Moreover, studies have suggested that SF-tuned mechanisms play a crucial role in size perception (Carrasco et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Neurons responding to peripheral stimulation are typically tuned to lower SFs than those representing central vision.
source: Neurons responding to peripheral stimulation are typically tuned to lower SFs than those representing central vision, and vice versa (Aghajari et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: SF-tuned neurons in the primary visual cortex are roughly scaled versions of one another in terms of their preferred SF, suggesting scale-invariance in neuronal processing of SF.
source: In addition, SF-tuned neurons in the primary visual cortex are roughly scaled versions of one another in terms of their preferred SF, suggesting scale-invariance in neuronal processing of SF (Teichert et al., 2007; also see Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is a link between the SF selectivity of neuronal populations and their receptive field sizes.
source: Based on these observations, one might infer a link between the SF selectivity of neuronal populations and their receptive field sizes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations described in the preceding text.

claim: Single-unit recordings from the striate cortex of macaques support a connection between SF selectivity and receptive field sizes.
source: Such a connection is supported by single-unit recordings from the striate cortex of macaques (De Valois et al., 1982; Foster et al., 1985) and cats (Movshon et al., 1978; Linsenmeier et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Single-unit recordings from the striate cortex of cats support a connection between SF selectivity and receptive field sizes.
source: Such a connection is supported by single-unit recordings from the striate cortex of macaques (De Valois et al., 1982; Foster et al., 1985) and cats (Movshon et al., 1978; Linsenmeier et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Keliris et al., 2019 introduced a novel method for estimating neuronal receptive field sizes in humans through fMRI, utilizing the SF selectivity of neurons.
source: Furthermore, extending these findings (Keliris et al., 2019) introduced a novel method for estimating neuronal receptive field sizes in humans through fMRI, utilizing the SF selectivity of neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The results from Keliris et al., 2019 were in close alignment with those obtained from electrophysiological measurements.
source: The results they provided were in close alignment with those obtained from electrophysiological measurements, yet they diverged significantly from pRF estimates.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from a cited study.

claim: The results from Keliris et al., 2019 diverged significantly from pRF estimates.
source: The results they provided were in close alignment with those obtained from electrophysiological measurements, yet they diverged significantly from pRF estimates.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from a cited study.

claim: pRF estimation remains a widely employed technique in human research.
source: While pRF estimation does not yield a direct measurement of neuronal receptive fields, it remains a widely employed technique in human research, spanning a diverse array of studies, including, but not limited to mapping the visual field (Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008; Amano et al., 2009), identifying neural correlates of visual performance and functioning (Silva et al., 2021; Harvey et al., 2015; He et al., 2019; Shen et al., 2020; Vo et al., 2017; Dekker et al., 2019), and examining how visual processing in the patient population diverges from the healthy population (Papanikolaou et al., 2014; Alvarez et al., 2020; Schwarzkopf et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies using pRF mapping.

claim: No existing study has elucidated how the interplay between neuronal RF size and SF selectivity is reflected in pRF estimates.
source: To our knowledge, no existing study has elucidated how the interplay between neuronal RF size and SF selectivity is reflected in pRF estimates.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: The protocols and procedures were approved by the University of Auckland Human Participants Ethics Committee (reference 024231).
source: The protocols and procedures were approved by the University of Auckland Human Participants Ethics Committee (reference 024231).
evidence: This is a direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: All participants gave their informed consent prior to the experiment.
source: All participants gave their informed consent prior to the experiment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the consent process.

claim: Participants used a chin rest to stabilize their heads 298 cm in front of a 4 K 65-inch monitor.
source: Participants used a chin rest to stabilize their heads 298 cm in front of a 4 K 65-inch monitor (LG webOS TV OLED 65E6T, 60 Hz refresh rate, 4096 × 2160 resolution).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental setup.

claim: The low SF adapter had a peak SF of 0.5 cpd.
source: One used low SF noise, which had a peak SF of 0.5 cpd, and the other used high SF noise with a peak SF of 3.5 cpd.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus parameters.

claim: The high SF adapter had a peak SF of 3.5 cpd.
source: One used low SF noise, which had a peak SF of 0.5 cpd, and the other used high SF noise with a peak SF of 3.5 cpd.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus parameters.

claim: The reference stimulus had a peak SF of approximately 1.3 cpd, the geometric mean of the SFs of the two adapters.
source: The one in the same visual hemifield as the adapter was called reference, and its peak SF was always ∼ 1.3 cpd, the geometric mean of the SFs of the two adapters.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus parameters.

claim: On average, the perceived SF of the reference stimulus was 7% higher under the low SF adaptation condition.
source: On average, the perceived SF of the reference stimulus (compared to the veridical mid-SF) was 7% higher, 13% lower, and 0.03% higher, respectively, under the low SF adaptation, high SF adaptation, and no-adaptation conditions (see Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claim: On average, the perceived SF of the reference stimulus was 13% lower under the high SF adaptation condition.
source: On average, the perceived SF of the reference stimulus (compared to the veridical mid-SF) was 7% higher, 13% lower, and 0.03% higher, respectively, under the low SF adaptation, high SF adaptation, and no-adaptation conditions (see Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claim: On average, the perceived SF of the reference stimulus was 0.03% higher under the no-adaptation condition.
source: On average, the perceived SF of the reference stimulus (compared to the veridical mid-SF) was 7% higher, 13% lower, and 0.03% higher, respectively, under the low SF adaptation, high SF adaptation, and no-adaptation conditions (see Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claim: The illusion magnitudes were not significantly different between the two visual hemifields.
source: Additionally, we found that the illusion magnitudes were not significantly different between the two visual hemifields (see appendix A.6 'Does the perceptual effect differ between the two visual hemifields?').
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claim: Behavioural results are consistent with previous studies on SF adaptation.
source: Our behavioural results are consistent with previous studies on SF adaptation (Blakemore and Sutton, 1969; Blakemore et al., 1970), as well as a variety of other studies on visual adaptation to size (Altan and Boyaci, 2020; Pooresmaeili et al., 2013), shape (Suzuki and Cavanagh, 1998; Storrs and Arnold, 2017), texture density (Sun et al., 2017), and motion (Mather et al., 2008), in terms of the bidirectional repulsive shift in perception of the adapted stimulus feature.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: 8 of the 10 volunteers from the psychophysics experiment participated in the fMRI experiment.
source: Therefore, 8 of the 10 volunteers from the psychophysics experiment participated in the fMRI experiment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study participants.

claim: The viewing distance in the fMRI experiment was 111 cm.
source: The viewing distance was 111 cm.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental setup.

claim: Each mapping run started with a 25 s baseline.
source: Each mapping run started with a 25 s baseline in which only the fixation point was shown on a gray background.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: The initial adaptation period was 30 s.
source: This was followed by the initial adaptation period of 30 s.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: Half of the runs included a high-SF adapter on the left and a low-SF adapter on the right visual hemifield (High-Low or HL runs).
source: This way, half of the runs included a high-SF adapter on the left and a low-SF adapter on the right visual hemifield (High-Low or HL runs), and the other half included the opposite configuration (Low-High or LH runs).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: The other half of the runs included the opposite configuration (Low-High or LH runs).
source: This way, half of the runs included a high-SF adapter on the left and a low-SF adapter on the right visual hemifield (High-Low or HL runs), and the other half included the opposite configuration (Low-High or LH runs).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: The bars were presented for 0.5 s and preceded by a 0.5 s of top-up adaptation.
source: The bars were presented for 0.5 s and preceded by a 0.5 s of top-up adaptation (this makes the effective initial adaptation period 30.5 s).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: MR images were collected at the Centre for Advanced Magnetic Resonance Imaging (CAMRI) in the Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences, the University of Auckland.
source: MR images were collected at the Centre for Advanced Magnetic Resonance Imaging (CAMRI) in the Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences, the University of Auckland.
evidence: This is a direct statement about where data was collected.

claim: A 3 Tesla MAGNETOM Skyra MR scanner was used.
source: We used a 3 Tesla MAGNETOM Skyra MR scanner (Siemens Healthcare, Erlangen, Germany).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the equipment used.

claim: The overall pRF sizes on the high SF adapted condition seem larger than those on the low SF adapted condition.
source: A visual inspection on the pRF size maps in Figure 4c clearly shows a difference between the two conditions, which is evident in all regions. The overall pRF sizes on the high SF adapted condition seem larger (less blue, more pink, and yellow) than those on the low SF adapted condition.
evidence: This is based on visual inspection of Figure 4c.

claim: On average, the median pRF sizes were larger in the high SF adaptation condition than in the low SF adaptation condition in all ROIs.
source: On average, the median pRF sizes were larger in the high SF adaptation condition than in the low SF adaptation condition in all ROIs (gray diamonds).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: In V1, six out of eight participants showed significantly larger pRF sizes in the high SF adapted condition as compared to those in the low SF adapted condition.
source: In V1, six out of eight participants showed significantly larger pRF sizes in the high SF adapted condition as compared to those in the low SF adapted condition (V2: 8 of 8, V3: 5 of 8, V4: 6 of 8, and V3A: 4 of 8).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical analysis results.

claim: In V2, all eight participants showed significantly larger pRF sizes in the high SF adapted condition as compared to those in the low SF adapted condition.
source: In V1, six out of eight participants showed significantly larger pRF sizes in the high SF adapted condition as compared to those in the low SF adapted condition (V2: 8 of 8, V3: 5 of 8, V4: 6 of 8, and V3A: 4 of 8).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical analysis results.

claim: In V3, five out of eight participants showed significantly larger pRF sizes in the high SF adapted condition as compared to those in the low SF adapted condition.
source: In V1, six out of eight participants showed significantly larger pRF sizes in the high SF adapted condition as compared to those in the low SF adapted condition (V2: 8 of 8, V3: 5 of 8, V4: 6 of 8, and V3A: 4 of 8).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical analysis results.

claim: In V4, six out of eight participants showed significantly larger pRF sizes in the high SF adapted condition as compared to those in the low SF adapted condition.
source: In V1, six out of eight participants showed significantly larger pRF sizes in the high SF adapted condition as compared to those in the low SF adapted condition (V2: 8 of 8, V3: 5 of 8, V4: 6 of 8, and V3A: 4 of 8).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical analysis results.

claim: In V3A, four out of eight participants showed significantly larger pRF sizes in the high SF adapted condition as compared to those in the low SF adapted condition.
source: In V1, six out of eight participants showed significantly larger pRF sizes in the high SF adapted condition as compared to those in the low SF adapted condition (V2: 8 of 8, V3: 5 of 8, V4: 6 of 8, and V3A: 4 of 8).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical analysis results.

claim: The difference plots were consistently above zero along almost all eccentricity bins in all visual regions.
source: The difference plots were consistently above zero along almost all eccentricity bins in all visual regions.
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: On average, the median pRF size in the high SF adapted condition was larger than in the low SF adapted condition in all regions and eccentricities.
source: This indicates that, on average, the median pRF size in the high SF adapted condition was larger than in the low SF adapted condition in all regions and eccentricities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: All participants successfully responded to most of the color events within 1 s.
source: The analysis for the performance of participants in responding to the fixation point color change showed that all participants successfully responded to most of the color events within 1 s.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the behavioral performance results.

claim: Stimulus contrast alters the receptive fields of visual neurons such that receptive fields expand in response to low-contrast stimuli and contract in response to high-contrast stimuli.
source: Stimulus contrast alters the receptive fields of visual neurons such that receptive fields (measured with mid-contrast grating stimuli) expand in response to low-contrast stimuli and contract in response to high-contrast stimuli (Sceniak et al., 1999; Kapadia et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Five participants in the contrast control experiment were recruited from the fMRI experiment.
source: Five were recruited from the fMRI experiment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study participants.

claim: The change in receptive field size observed after SF adaptation cannot be explained by possible perceived contrast differences caused by the high and low SF adapters.
source: Results suggest that the change in receptive field size we observed after SF adaptation cannot be explained by possible perceived contrast differences caused by our high and low SF adapters.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the results of the contrast control experiment.

claim: The findings provide novel empirical evidence of the relationship between SF tuning and pRF sizes in humans.
source: In this study, we provide novel empirical evidence of this relationship by incorporating an adaptation paradigm into the standard pRF mapping procedure.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty and contribution of the study.

claim: Adapting to a band-pass SF noise pattern results in a shift in the pRF size distributions in the early visual areas.
source: Our results demonstrated that adapting to a band-pass SF noise pattern results in (1) a shift in the pRF size distributions in the early visual areas, and (2) a repulsive perceptual SF aftereffect on the subsequently presented pattern.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Adapting to a band-pass SF noise pattern results in a repulsive perceptual SF aftereffect on the subsequently presented pattern.
source: Our results demonstrated that adapting to a band-pass SF noise pattern results in (1) a shift in the pRF size distributions in the early visual areas, and (2) a repulsive perceptual SF aftereffect on the subsequently presented pattern.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The behavioral effect found is consistent with previous adaptation studies.
source: The behavioral effect we found is consistent with previous adaptation studies (Blakemore and Sutton, 1969; Blakemore et al., 1970).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The spatial tuning of neuronal populations was sharpened following a low-SF adaptation.
source: Most importantly, our fMRI experiment showed that in multiple visual regions, ranging from V1 to V3A and V4, the spatial tuning of neuronal populations was sharpened following a low-SF adaptation and broadened after a high-SF adaptation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The spatial tuning of neuronal populations was broadened after a high-SF adaptation.
source: Most importantly, our fMRI experiment showed that in multiple visual regions, ranging from V1 to V3A and V4, the spatial tuning of neuronal populations was sharpened following a low-SF adaptation and broadened after a high-SF adaptation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Population receptive field sizes in the early visual cortical regions are linked to the SF selectivity of visual neurons.
source: This provides evidence that population receptive field sizes in the early visual cortical regions are linked to the SF selectivity of visual neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the main findings of the study.

claim: The relationship shown between pRF sizes and SF tuning of neuronal populations aligns with early studies that reported a correlation between the preferred SF and classical receptive field size in the animal striate cortex.
source: The relationship we showed between pRF sizes and SF tuning of neuronal populations aligns with early studies that reported a correlation between the preferred SF and classical receptive field size in the animal striate cortex (e.g. De Valois et al., 1982; Movshon et al., 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Keliris et al., 2019's fMRI findings on humans suggested larger/smaller average single-unit receptive field (suRF) sizes for the checkerboard stimuli containing a lower/higher SF pattern, respectively.
source: In addition, Keliris et al., 2019's fMRI findings on humans suggested larger/smaller average single-unit receptive field (suRF) sizes for the checkerboard stimuli containing a lower/higher SF pattern, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from a cited study.

claim: Keliris et al., 2019's results are directly comparable to electrophysiology studies because they estimated SF-dependent BOLD response and eliminated spatial scatter of the receptive fields.
source: Importantly (as they also argued) their results are directly comparable to electrophysiology studies because they estimated SF-dependent BOLD response and eliminated spatial scatter of the receptive fields.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology and interpretation of a cited study.

claim: A previous fMRI study found no evidence of SF-selectivity-dependent pRF size change.
source: Nevertheless, and contrary to our findings, a previous fMRI study has found no evidence of SF-selectivity-dependent pRF size change (Welbourne et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about findings from a cited study.

claim: Welbourne et al., 2018 found no difference between pRF estimates made with an achromatic luminance-defined grating and with either of two isoluminant chromatic gratings.
source: They found no difference between pRF estimates made with an achromatic luminance-defined grating and with either of two isoluminant chromatic gratings, and suggested that the receptive field size and SF tuning coupling does not hold at the cortical level.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from a cited study.

claim: Previous studies established that pRFs could be estimated with occluded as well as illusory contour stimuli.
source: Previous studies established that pRFs could be estimated with occluded as well as illusory contour stimuli (de Haas and Schwarzkopf, 2018) and with motion-defined bar stimuli (Hughes et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous studies established that pRFs could be estimated with motion-defined bar stimuli.
source: Previous studies established that pRFs could be estimated with occluded as well as illusory contour stimuli (de Haas and Schwarzkopf, 2018) and with motion-defined bar stimuli (Hughes et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The responses obtained from the mapping stimuli are dominated by a more complex processing rather than the specific stimulus properties.
source: These findings suggest that the responses obtained from the mapping stimuli are dominated by a more complex processing rather than the specific stimulus properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies.

claim: The difference in the pRF estimations would inherently originate from SF adaptation.
source: In the present study, we used the same mapping stimuli between conditions. The difference in the pRF estimations would inherently originate from SF adaptation, which not only showed a strong perceptual effect (psychophysical experiment) but also likely had a robust effect on the responsiveness of the relevant neuronal populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design and results.

claim: The brief adaptation was enough to yield a strong perceptual effect behaviorally.
source: Although this brief adaptation was enough to yield a strong perceptual effect behaviorally, it might raise questions about whether the observed pRF size change can possibly be related to such a short adaptation.
evidence: This is based on the results of the psychophysical experiment.

claim: The effective adaptation duration consistently exceeded that of a single top-up presentation in the fMRI experiment.
source: This accumulation occurs because the entire visual field we measured was consistently stimulated by the adaptation stimuli, while the mapping stimulus only covered a small portion in any given trial, and it varied in size and location throughout the run. This design ensured that the effective adaptation duration consistently exceeded that of a single top-up presentation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design.

claim: The adaptation effect in the fMRI experiment was likely more pronounced than what was quantified behaviorally.
source: Consequently, it can also be inferred that the adaptation effect in our fMRI experiment was likely more pronounced than what we quantified behaviorally.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design.

claim: Both percent signal change time series and noise ceiling data from each vertex indicate similar SNR between the conditions.
source: Both percent signal change time series and noise ceiling data from each vertex indicate similar SNR between the conditions.
evidence: This is based on supplementary analyses mentioned in the text.

claim: The control experiment demonstrated that the observed differences between the two adaptation conditions cannot be attributed to differences in perceived contrast.
source: Our control experiment demonstrated that the observed differences between the two adaptation conditions cannot be attributed to differences in perceived contrast.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the results of the control experiment.

claim: SF adaptation increases the detection threshold of same-SF test stimuli viewed subsequently, with this effect gradually fading for test SFs that are increasingly different from the adapted SF, until the difference reaches 2 octaves.
source: Previous research has indicated that SF adaptation increases the detection threshold of same-SF test stimuli viewed subsequently, with this effect gradually fading for test SFs that are increasingly different from the adapted SF, until the difference reaches 2 octaves (Snowden and Hammett, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The magnitude of the perceptual aftereffect was higher after the high SF adapter, as compared to that after the low SF adapter.
source: While the perceived contrast following the two adapters showed no differences, a noteworthy difference was observed in the SF aftereffect. The magnitude of the perceptual aftereffect was higher after the high SF adapter, as compared to that after the low SF adapter.
